sims.title: One set, three notations
sims.intro: The midterm asks for the same answer three times — graphed, in set-builder notation and in interval notation — and marks each of them separately. They are one object with three spellings, and this is that object. Drag the endpoints, decide whether each is included, and switch between shading *between* them and shading *outside* them.
watch: Change `left end included` from 0 to 1 and watch two things move together: the circle fills in, and the round bracket in the interval becomes square. They are the same fact written twice, which is why losing one of them loses a mark on its own.

Set `shade outside` to 1. The single interval becomes two rays joined with $\cup$, and the set-builder line changes its **and** into an **or**. That switch is the whole content of $\lvert u\rvert<k$ against $\lvert u\rvert>k$ in §1.7.
With `shade outside` on, notice that the endpoints swap: the rays keep the endpoint exactly when the middle gives it up. A set and its complement cannot both own the same boundary point.
Whatever you do to the sliders, the infinite end never takes a square bracket. $\infty$ is not a number and cannot be included — the reason $[3,\infty]$ is marked wrong every time.
Set both endpoints to the same number with neither included: the interval collapses to $\varnothing$. An empty answer is still an answer, and it has its own symbol.

challenges.prompt: Build the solution set of $x>\tfrac87$ — one of the answers from §1.7. Put the left endpoint at 1, leave the right at 9, exclude the left end and include the right, shading between.
challenges.explain: The readout shows $(1.00, 9.00]$ — an open left end and a closed right end. A genuine $x>\tfrac87$ runs to infinity on the right, which the slider cannot reach; what this drill fixes is the **left** end, where a $>$ always produces a round bracket. On the paper the same set is written $\left(\tfrac87,\infty\right)$, round at both ends.

challenges.prompt: Now produce the shape of $\lvert 3x-6\rvert>9$ from §1.7: endpoints at $-1$ and $5$, neither included, shaded outside.
challenges.explain: The readout reads $(-\infty, -1.00) \cup (5.00, \infty)$ and calls the shape *two rays (an 'or')*. Compare it with the same endpoints shaded **between**, which is $(-1,5)$ — the answer a student gets by treating a greater-than like a less-than. The two sets share not a single point: getting the split wrong does not cost you part of the answer, it costs you all of it.

challenges.prompt: Make the set $[-6,0]$ — the answer to $5\lvert x+3\rvert-2\le13$ in the problems tab.
challenges.explain: Both circles are filled and both brackets are square, because the inequality was $\le$ rather than $<$. Read the set-builder line the scene prints: $\{x \mid -6.00 \le x \le 0.00\}$. That is the third notation the paper wants, and it is free once the graph is right.

sims.title: Why less-than gives one interval and greater-than gives two
sims.intro: $\lvert x-a\rvert$ is the distance from $x$ to $a$, and its graph is a wedge with its point at $a$. Cutting that wedge with the horizontal line $y=k$ is the whole of §1.7's absolute-value rule: below the line is one stretch, above it is two. Slide $a$ to move the wedge, $k$ to move the cut, and the last slider to change which side of the cut you want.
watch: With the direction at $<$, the shaded part of the $x$-axis is the piece **under** the wedge — one interval, centred on $a$. That is the *and* case: $-k<x-a<k$.

Flip the direction to $>$ without touching anything else. The shading jumps to the two outer pieces. Nothing about the picture changed except which side of the line you asked for, and the answer went from one interval to two rays.
Move $k$ down to $0$. The two rays close in until they meet at the vertex, and the single interval disappears. At $k=0$ the equation $\lvert x-a\rvert=0$ has exactly one solution, $x=a$.

Push $k$ **below** zero. Now the line lies under the vertex and the wedge never reaches it: with $<$ the answer is $\varnothing$, with $>$ it is every real number. The lecture slides state the rule only for $k>0$ and stop there; a paper does not always oblige, and both of these have been asked.
Move $a$ and watch the solution slide with it while its **width** stays $2k$. The centre comes from the expression inside the bars; the width comes from the constant outside them.

challenges.prompt: Set up $\lvert x-2\rvert<3$ and read the solution.
challenges.explain: The readout gives $(-1.00, 5.00)$ and names the shape *one interval (an 'and')*. Written out, the split is $-3<x-2<3$: add 2 throughout and you have the interval. Notice the scene also prints that split for you — on a paper it is the line that earns the method mark.

challenges.prompt: Keep the same wedge and the same cut, and switch the direction to $>$.
challenges.explain: The answer is now $(-\infty,-1.00)\cup(5.00,\infty)$: the *complement* of what you had a moment ago, apart from the two endpoints. This is the single most expensive error in §1.7 — a student who splits a greater-than like a less-than does not lose part of the answer, they hand in the exact set of values that fail.

challenges.prompt: Now drop the constant below zero with the direction still at $>$: set $k=-3$.
challenges.explain: The scene reads *always true: a distance is never negative* and gives $(-\infty,\infty)$. The line sits below the point of the wedge, so **every** $x$ satisfies it. Swap the direction to $<$ with $k$ still negative and you get $\varnothing$ for the same reason read the other way. Neither case has a boundary point, which is why splitting them into two equations produces nonsense.

challenges.prompt: Return to $<$ and set the centre to $-4$ with $k=2$.
challenges.explain: The solution $(-6.00,-2.00)$ is still $2k=4$ wide, just recentred. The centre of an absolute-value solution is always the value that makes the inside zero — here $x=-4$ — which is a two-second check on any answer you write.

sims.title: What squaring does to a radical equation

params.label: the constant c in x + c

sims.intro: Squaring both sides is not a reversible step, and this is what that sentence means. The dark curve is $y=\sqrt{x+6}$; the green line is $y=x+c$. Solving $\sqrt{x+6}=x+c$ by squaring produces the roots of $x^{2}+(2c-1)x+(c^{2}-6)=0$ — but only the ones where the two graphs **actually cross** are solutions. Slide $c$ and watch candidates appear, get kept, and get thrown away.
watch: A filled point is a genuine solution: the curve and the line meet there. A hollow point is a candidate that solves the squared equation and not the original — the line has gone below the axis, and a principal square root is never negative.

The two curves can only meet where $x\ge-6$ (the radical must be defined) **and** where $x+c\ge0$ (the right-hand side cannot be negative). Those two conditions are exactly the check you are told to perform by hand.
Push $c$ up to 3 or beyond: the line rises clear of the curve, the discriminant goes negative, and there are no candidates at all. "No real solution" is a real answer, not a failure to find one.

At some settings **both** candidates survive. Checking is not a ritual for finding a root to throw away — it is how you learn which candidates are solutions, and sometimes the answer is all of them (problem 9 in the problems tab is exactly that case).

Notice that the squared equation never knows anything is wrong. Its roots are perfectly good numbers; it is only the original equation that can tell them apart. That is why the check has to be done in the original.

challenges.explain: Squaring gives $x^{2}-x-6=0$, so the candidates are $-2$ and $3$. The scene keeps $3$ and rejects $-2$: at $x=-2$ the left-hand side is $\sqrt4=2$ and the right-hand side is $-2$. Same magnitude, wrong sign — and squaring is exactly the operation that cannot tell those apart.

The candidates are about $1.30$ and $7.70$, and only $7.70$ survives. Again the rejected one is where the line is below the axis. Note that this happened without any arithmetic mistake anywhere — an unchecked answer of "$x\approx1.30$ and $x\approx7.70$" is wrong on a paper that has been marked correctly all the way down.

challenges.prompt: Push $c$ to $4$ and read the discriminant.
challenges.explain: The discriminant is negative, so the squared equation has no real roots and the line never meets the curve. The answer to write is "no real solution" — and notice you could have seen it from the picture before doing any algebra, because the line is above the curve everywhere.
